title: The Late Postcards
premise: Sable Dravenmoor, a night librarian in an insomniac city, learns that the house where she grew up — and from which she was quietly sent away at nine years old — is being auctioned by a stranger claiming kinship. Sorting the estate's boxes, she finds postcards mailed to her over twenty years by her estranged mother, all returned unopened, and realizes the woman she cast as villain was writing to her all along. As Sable traces the sender through the city's fading neighborhoods, she must decide whether loyalty to her adoptive family's version of events matters more than the truth of who abandoned whom. In the end, she lets the house go to strangers but claims the postcards and her mother's final unfinished letter, choosing truth over inherited grievance and finally belonging to herself.
about_author: Kestrel Ravensworth is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing other people's letters before writing her own. She lives in a coastal city that never quite sleeps and writes at night, when the post offices are closed.

chapters.title: The Hours Between
chapters.summary: POV Sable. A night shift at the Halcyon Branch Library establishes Sable's tenant-like existence: she catalogs lives in books while avoiding her own, sleeping days in a rented room. When a legal notice arrives naming the Dravenmoor house as auction property, her carefully ordered nights crack open. Emotional beat: restless unease disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Lot 47
chapters.summary: POV Sable. She attends the pre-auction viewing and walks the rooms of her childhood, now staged for strangers. The claimant, a brisk man named Aldous Vane, calls himself a distant cousin with papers to prove it. She finds one box mislabeled with her name. Emotional beat: vertigo — the past asserting ownership of her.

chapters.title: Returned to Sender
chapters.summary: POV Sable. In the box: dozens of postcards addressed to her across two decades, each stamped undeliverable, sent from her mother Marisol — the woman her adoptive aunt swore had abandoned her without a word. The handwriting shifts, ages, persists. Emotional beat: betrayal of everything she believed about her own history.

chapters.title: The Aunt's Version
chapters.summary: POV Sable, with flashback. Sable confronts Aunt Corliss, now frail, who repeats the old story: Marisol was unstable, unfit, gone. But Corliss's certainty has hairline fractures, and a locked cedar chest she refuses to open. Emotional beat: loyalty tested against doubt; love as a kind of censorship.

chapters.title: Postmarks
chapters.summary: POV Sable. Mapping the postcards' origins, she follows their route through the city — a diner, a shuttered hotel, a laundromat — interviewing people who knew Marisol. Each remembers a woman who wrote every week and asked only if the letters arrived. Emotional beat: grief curdling into anger at whoever intercepted them.

chapters.title: Aldous Vane's Papers
chapters.summary: POV Sable. Investigating Vane's claim, Sable discovers his 'kinship documents' are forged — he's a speculator flipping the house, exploiting a dead estate. But buried in his paperwork is a genuine document: guardianship papers signed by Corliss, dated before Marisol ever left town. Emotional beat: the ground tilts; the villain may be family.

chapters.title: What Corliss Kept
chapters.summary: POV Sable. Corliss, confronted, finally opens the cedar chest: every reply Sable ever sent as a child, plus the court order Corliss obtained by exaggerating Marisol's illness. 'I was keeping you safe,' she says, 'from a life like mine.' Emotional beat: climax of the loyalty-vs-truth theme — forgiveness begins as comprehension.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: POV Sable. Auction day. Vane expects no competition; Sable arrives not to bid on the house but to read Marisol's last returned postcard aloud to the assembled crowd — a public reclaiming of the record. The house sells, but the story of it changes hands too. Emotional beat: quiet triumph; truth spoken in a room built for transactions.

chapters.title: Unfinished Letter
chapters.summary: POV Sable. Among the postcards is a final envelope, sealed, unsent — Marisol died two winters ago. Inside: an unfinished letter asking not for forgiveness but for one meeting, and an address. Sable goes; the room is empty, kept by a landlady who hands over a notebook Marisol left 'for the girl, if she ever comes.' Emotional beat: mourning and tenderness entwined.

chapters.title: Owner of Small Things
chapters.summary: POV Sable. Weeks later, Sable reads Marisol's notebook at the library desk where she works, then writes her first letter in twenty years — to the landlady, to Corliss, to herself. She keeps the postcards in a shoebox labeled with her own name, no longer a tenant of her past. Emotional beat: resolution — belonging claimed, not granted.
